“Ladies in the locker room are not women who think they know everything about sports; they just know the men who do,” Lemon said.

That line is one of the slogans she uses to explain the show, and it tends to lower the guard of skeptics who might otherwise dismiss an all-women sports program.

“It’s all women, all sports, all sexy,” Lemon said. “It’s a combination of my love of sports and my love of media.”

For each of the past five years, Lemon has assembled a fresh cast of on-air personalities and production staff to create roughly six episodes. The program is recorded live at sports bars and restaurants around the Atlanta metropolitan area, while studio time is also used to produce additional segments for the show.

For the second time since the program began, Lemon is heading to the Super Bowl with several of the women from the show and a production team. There, they plan to produce a special edition featuring interviews with celebrities and prominent figures drawn to football’s biggest event.

Soma Balber, who describes herself as a devoted Los Angeles Lakers fan, served as one of the show’s commentators during the 2008-09 season. “It’s kind of nice to show the audience that women can have fun watching sports,” Balber said. “And we want to educate women about sports as well.”

Lemon, who says she is a major fan of professional football, hopes the program helps more men recognize that women are sports fans, too.

“When women talk about sports, sometimes men look at us as groupies,” Lemon said. “Men don’t think women understand sports.”

She added that men who have never played sports but still know every statistic are often accepted without question — they are given what she calls the “man pass.” Lemon says that may not be fair, but “it is what it is. I just hope we get more women talking about sports.”

# Atlanta’s “Ladies in the Locker Room” is changing who gets to talk sports

**By [Reporter Name]**

**ATLANTA —** In a city where sports talk often sounds like a familiar boys’ club, Hattie Lemon wanted to build a different kind of room — one where women weren’t guests, side notes or afterthoughts.

So she created **“Ladies in the Locker Room,”** an Atlanta-based, all-female sports commentary show that blends game analysis, cultural conversation and the kind of unfiltered banter usually reserved for barbershops, tailgates and postgame group chats.

“We’re not here to prove that women know sports,” Lemon said. “We already do. We’re here to create a platform where our voices are the standard, not the exception.”

The show, founded by Lemon, brings together women with distinct perspectives on football, basketball, baseball, sports culture and the business of athletics. From Atlanta Falcons breakdowns to WNBA storylines, from college football rivalries to conversations about athletes as entrepreneurs and activists, “Ladies in the Locker Room” aims to cover sports with both expertise and personality.

For Lemon, the mission is personal.

“I grew up loving the game, debating the game, watching the game,” she said. “But when I turned on a lot of sports shows, I didn’t always see women who looked like me or sounded like me leading the conversation. I wanted to change that.”

## Building a sports platform in Atlanta

Atlanta is a fitting home base for the show. The city has long been a cultural and sports crossroads — home to major professional franchises, powerhouse college programs, passionate fan bases and a thriving media and entertainment scene.

It is also a city where Black women have been central to entrepreneurship, culture and community leadership. Lemon says that energy helped shape the identity of “Ladies in the Locker Room.”

“Atlanta gives you permission to build,” she said. “This city is full of people who create lanes when the traditional doors don’t open. That’s what we’re doing in sports media.”

The show’s title is intentional. “Locker room” conversations are often associated with players, coaches and male commentators. Lemon wanted to reclaim the phrase and expand its meaning.

“When people hear ‘locker room,’ they think access,” she said. “They think honesty. They think strategy. We wanted to say: women belong in that space, too — not as visitors, but as voices who can lead.”

## More than scores and stats

While the show covers the numbers — scores, standings, injuries, trades and matchups — Lemon says the heart of “Ladies in the Locker Room” is the conversation around the game.

That includes how athletes navigate fame, mental health, family, race, gender and finances. It also includes the way fans experience sports as part of everyday life.

“Sports is never just sports,” Lemon said. “It’s culture. It’s business. It’s identity. It’s who gets paid, who gets protected, who gets criticized and who gets celebrated.”

The show’s all-female format is not a gimmick, Lemon says. It is a response to a media landscape where women sports commentators are often judged differently than their male peers.

“A man can be loud, funny, wrong, passionate, emotional — and it’s entertainment,” she said. “A woman does the same thing and suddenly people question whether she belongs. We’re pushing back on that.”

The show also challenges the idea that women’s sports commentary must be limited to women’s sports.

“We love women’s sports, and we’re absolutely going to talk about them,” Lemon said. “But we’re also going to talk NFL. We’re going to talk NBA. We’re going to talk college football. We’re going to talk everything — because women watch everything.”

## Creating space for new voices

For emerging women in sports media, visibility can be just as important as opportunity. Lemon says part of the show’s purpose is to become a platform where women can sharpen their voices, build audiences and enter broader conversations in the industry.

“You can’t become what you never see,” she said. “If a young girl in Atlanta sees us debating a fourth-down call or breaking down a playoff series, maybe she starts thinking, ‘I can do that.’ That matters.”

The show’s format leaves room for disagreement — something Lemon says is essential to authentic commentary.

“We don’t all have to agree,” she said. “That’s what makes it good. Sports talk is supposed to be passionate. It’s supposed to have different angles. We can debate hard and still respect each other.”

In that way, “Ladies in the Locker Room” reflects the spirit of modern sports fandom: fast-moving, opinionated, social media-driven and deeply connected to identity.

A single segment might move from a Falcons performance review to a discussion about NIL deals, then shift into how female athletes are marketed compared with male athletes. Lemon says that range is the point.

“Our audience is smart,” she said. “They don’t need us to water anything down. They want real opinions, real analysis and real conversation.”

## A larger shift in sports media

The rise of “Ladies in the Locker Room” comes amid a broader transformation in sports media. Women are increasingly visible as analysts, reporters, podcast hosts, producers and executives. Yet barriers remain, from online harassment to unequal opportunities behind the desk and in decision-making roles.

Lemon says representation cannot stop at simply adding one woman to an existing panel.

“One seat is not enough,” she said. “We need shows. We need ownership. We need production power. We need to be in the room when decisions are made about what stories matter.”

That philosophy shapes how she thinks about the show’s future. Lemon wants “Ladies in the Locker Room” to grow beyond commentary into live events, community partnerships, athlete interviews and mentorship opportunities for young women interested in sports media.

“The vision is bigger than a show,” she said. “It’s a movement. It’s a network. It’s a place where women can talk sports, build careers and open doors for the next woman coming behind them.”

## Changing the conversation

For now, Lemon says the most rewarding feedback comes from viewers who say the show makes them feel seen.

Some are lifelong sports fans who are tired of being underestimated. Others are casual fans who feel welcomed by a conversation that is knowledgeable without being exclusionary. And some are young women imagining a future in front of the camera, behind the microphone or inside a production booth.

“That’s why we do it,” Lemon said. “Every time someone says, ‘I needed this,’ it reminds us that the platform matters.”

In a crowded sports media landscape, “Ladies in the Locker Room” is betting that authenticity, perspective and community can cut through.

Lemon knows the show will still face skeptics. But she says skepticism is nothing new.

“Women have always had to fight to be heard in sports,” she said. “We’re not asking for permission anymore. We built our own locker room.”

And in Atlanta, the door is open.

**A new all-women sports analysis show is taking on the old boys’ club of sports talk**

In a media landscape where sports debate has long been dominated by loud male voices, a new all-women analysis program is trying to change not only who gets to talk about the game — but how the conversation sounds.

The show, hosted by Hattie Lemon and Soma Balber, blends sharp tactical breakdowns, league-wide analysis, athlete interviews and culture-forward commentary. But its bigger mission is clear: challenge the assumption that sports expertise has a default gender.

“We’re not here to be the ‘women’s version’ of anything,” Lemon said. “We’re here because we know the game, we study the game, and we have something to say that sports fans haven’t always been given the chance to hear.”

For decades, sports talk television has leaned heavily on a familiar format: aggressive debate, quick-fire takes and panels often made up almost entirely of men. Women have increasingly broken through as reporters, anchors, analysts and former athletes turned commentators, but many say the industry still treats women’s expertise as something to be proven again and again.

Balber said that pressure is part of what the show hopes to dismantle.

“There’s this exhausting expectation that women in sports media have to walk into every room with a résumé in one hand and a stat sheet in the other just to be believed,” Balber said. “We want to get past that. The analysis should stand on its own.”

The program arrives at a moment when women’s sports are drawing record ratings, expanding audiences and new investment — from the WNBA’s rising star power to the continued global growth of women’s soccer, college volleyball, gymnastics and beyond. But Lemon and Balber insist the show is not only about women’s sports.

That distinction matters to them.

“We’re going to talk about the NBA, the NFL, the Premier League, combat sports, tennis, college athletics — all of it,” Lemon said. “Women don’t only have authority when the subject is women’s sports. We’re fans and analysts of the entire sports world.”

The show’s format reflects that broader ambition. Segments include film-room style breakdowns, data-driven trend analysis, interviews with athletes and coaches, and roundtable conversations about the business and culture surrounding sports. Producers say the goal is to make room for both rigorous analysis and a different tone — one less dependent on manufactured outrage.

Balber said the show is not trying to eliminate debate, but to reframe it.

“Disagreement is part of sports. That’s what makes it fun,” she said. “But there’s a difference between arguing because you care about the details and shouting because the format rewards noise. We’re interested in the details.”

The show also leans into the personalities of its hosts. Lemon brings an energetic, conversational approach, often connecting on-field strategy to broader cultural narratives. Balber is more measured, with a reputation for precise analysis and a willingness to challenge conventional wisdom.

Together, they hope to create a space that feels accessible to casual viewers without talking down to dedicated fans.

“Sports can be emotional, technical, hilarious and heartbreaking all at once,” Lemon said. “We want the show to reflect that full range.”

Industry observers have noted that representation in sports media is about more than optics. Who gets to analyze games can shape which stories are elevated, which athletes are taken seriously and which fan communities feel invited into the conversation.

That’s especially important as the sports audience itself becomes more diverse. Women make up a large and growing portion of fan bases across major leagues, yet sports programming has often lagged behind that reality.

Balber said she hopes younger viewers see the show and understand that expertise does not have one look or sound.

“If a girl watches and thinks, ‘I could do that,’ that matters,” she said. “But I also hope men watch and just see good sports analysis. Because that’s the point. We belong in the main conversation, not a side conversation.”

The hosts know criticism will come. Women in sports media are often subject to disproportionate scrutiny and online harassment, particularly when expressing opinions about men’s leagues. Lemon said the team is prepared for that but refuses to let it define the project.

“We’re not building this show around fear of the comment section,” she said. “We’re building it around the audience that’s been waiting for something smarter, broader and more reflective of who sports fans actually are.”

For Lemon and Balber, the show’s success will not be measured only in ratings or viral clips, but in whether it helps normalize women as authoritative voices in sports analysis.

“The dream is that one day this isn’t treated as revolutionary,” Balber said. “It’s just a great sports show hosted by women who know what they’re talking about.”

Until then, Lemon said, they’re happy to keep pushing.

“Sports talk has had a pretty narrow definition for a long time,” she said. “We’re here to widen it.”

**Atlanta-Area Show “Ladies in the Locker Room” Gives Women Sports Fans a Mic — and a Mission**

In a sports culture where women are still too often treated as guests in the conversation, an Atlanta-area show is working to make one thing clear: women do not need permission to talk sports.

*Ladies in the Locker Room* has built its identity around a simple but powerful mission — proving that women know sports too. The show, rooted in the Atlanta area, brings women’s voices to the center of the game-day conversation, offering commentary, debate and fan perspective on the teams, athletes and storylines that move the sports world.

For many women sports fans, the show reflects a familiar experience: loving the game, following the stats, knowing the roster — and still being tested, doubted or talked over.

Whether at watch parties, sports bars, family gatherings or online forums, women often describe having to “prove” their fandom in ways men rarely do. A woman wearing a jersey may be quizzed on a team’s history. A woman offering an opinion on a coaching decision may be dismissed before she finishes her point. A woman working in sports media may face criticism not for what she says, but for being the one saying it.

*Ladies in the Locker Room* pushes back against that culture by creating a space where women are not an afterthought in sports talk — they are the analysts, the fans, the storytellers and the voices driving the conversation.

The show’s appeal lies not only in its sports coverage, but in its human side. It speaks to the women who grew up watching football with their fathers, learned basketball from older brothers, played softball, ran track, coached youth teams, managed fantasy leagues or simply fell in love with the drama of competition. It speaks to mothers raising daughters who now see women breaking barriers as referees, coaches, executives, broadcasters and athletes with growing visibility.

In Atlanta, a city with a deep and diverse sports identity, that mission carries particular weight. The area’s sports landscape includes passionate fan bases for professional, college and high school athletics. From football Saturdays to basketball rivalries and championship dreams, sports are part of the region’s rhythm. *Ladies in the Locker Room* taps into that energy while widening the lens on who gets to be heard.

The show also arrives at a time when women’s sports are experiencing historic momentum. Record television audiences, rising attendance and increased media coverage have helped shift the national conversation. Stars in basketball, soccer, tennis, gymnastics and track and field have inspired new generations of fans. But the growth of women’s sports has also highlighted a broader point: women have always been part of sports culture — as athletes, consumers, experts and loyal fans.

Still, representation in sports commentary remains uneven. While more women are appearing on national broadcasts and digital platforms, many continue to face stereotypes about credibility and expertise. Shows like *Ladies in the Locker Room* challenge those assumptions at the community level, where cultural change often begins.

The format gives women room to be passionate without apology. They can celebrate wins, question play-calling, critique front-office moves and debate the biggest headlines with the same intensity expected from any sports commentator. The difference is that the show’s very existence makes a statement: sports knowledge is not defined by gender.

For listeners and viewers, that message can be validating. A woman who has spent years defending her place in sports conversations may hear the show and feel seen. A young girl who loves stats and highlight reels may recognize that there is room for her voice too. Even male fans may find the show challenges old assumptions and opens the door to a broader, richer sports dialogue.

At its heart, *Ladies in the Locker Room* is not just about proving women know sports. It is about questioning why they were ever expected to prove it in the first place.

The show’s mission reflects a larger movement toward inclusion in sports media — one that does not ask women to choose between being fans and being taken seriously. It embraces the full range of sports fandom: the analysis, the emotion, the loyalty, the frustration, the joy.

And in doing so, *Ladies in the Locker Room* reminds Atlanta-area audiences that the locker room conversation belongs to everyone who loves the game.
